html:
The map's label, in 500 BCE, for the Iron Age peoples of South India and the Deccan, known mostly from their large stone graves. Similar burials were built from roughly 1200 BCE into the early centuries CE.

They buried their dead in stone circles, slab chambers, urns and rock-cut tombs, often with iron tools and weapons, horse gear, beads and black-and-red pottery. One well-known site is Adichanallur in Tamil Nadu. They farmed rice and millets, kept cattle and worked iron well.

These were probably the ancestors of the Dravidian-speaking peoples of the south. The early Tamil poems of Sangam literature describe burial customs that fit these graves, and the chiefdoms of this period grew into the kingdoms of the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas. They are a South Indian part of the worldwide megalith tradition, though not linked to it directly.
